messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem is a 54-year-old single man of Lebanese descent who works as a software engineer at a mid-sized technology firm in the Chicago area. He presents for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after a sexual assault that occurred in the parking structure adjacent to his office building. On a late evening when Kareem had stayed past midnight to meet a deployment deadline, two men in what he initially took to be security uniforms approached him as he walked to his car. One of them displayed what appeared to be a badge. Kareem, who had grown up navigating authority figures with careful deference, complied when they instructed him to stop. What followed was a prolonged assault in the concrete stairwell of the structure, punctuated by the distant wail of a passing ambulance that he has never been able to unhear. The men left without a word. Kareem drove home, showered, and did not report the assault. He was certain, in the hours and days that followed, that something in the way he had presented himself — his compliance, his willingness to follow their instruction, the fact that he had been alone so late — had invited what happened. That conviction has not loosened its grip.

In the weeks after the assault, Kareem began to reorganize his life around the geometry of threat. He stopped using the parking structure entirely and now parks four blocks away, adding a long detour that takes him nowhere near the building's eastern side. He will not enter any space where uniformed personnel are present — he has avoided the post office, declined a company all-hands meeting held in a building lobby staffed by security guards, and quietly stopped attending the quarterly technology conferences he once found professionally sustaining. When a police cruiser idles at the curb outside his apartment, he moves to the back of the building until it leaves. These adjustments accumulated quietly over months, each one feeling not like retreat but like reasonable precaution, until the radius of places where he could function had narrowed to his apartment and, on most days, his desk at work — provided he arrives early enough to be settled before colleagues fill the floor.

At work, the open-plan office has become a source of sustained vigilance. Kareem sits with his back to the wall and monitors the room continuously, tracking who enters and where they stand. When a male colleague stops by his desk to talk, Kareem manages the interaction with visible efficiency, ending it as quickly as courtesy allows. The idea of being alone in a room with a male colleague — in a conference room, in the elevator — produces a physical alertness that he describes as his body deciding things before his mind catches up. He has turned down two project lead opportunities in the past year because both would have required him to manage small teams and hold one-on-one meetings. His manager has noted the withdrawal and interpreted it as disengagement; their relationship, once collegial, has grown formal and cool.

Sirens reach him wherever he is. In the middle of a code review, the sound of an ambulance on the street below pulls him entirely out of the present. He does not always know, in those moments, where he is. The return to the room is effortful and leaves him hollowed.

What troubles Kareem most deeply, beyond the fear, is a conviction about what the experience has done to him permanently. He had come to believe, with a quiet certainty that he found more frightening than the intrusions themselves, that the capacity for ordinary feeling — warmth, connection, the modest pleasure he once took in his work — had simply been taken from him and would not return. Alongside this sits a grief that has nowhere to go: he knows that nothing has been done about what happened, that the men have never been identified, and the unfairness of that fact sits in him like something structural.

He sought help after his younger sister visited from Dearborn and told him, gently and directly, that she did not recognise him. He came to the intake session hoping, with considerable doubt, that he might be told he was not permanently changed. That is what he most wants to be wrong about.
